opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I joined NVIDIA, around 2016, I was coming from a background in computer vision, and I had watched what happened with image recognition. Within just a few years, deep learning went from an interesting idea to completely dominating benchmarks like ImageNet. Hand-engineered features that people had spent decades refining were suddenly outperformed by networks that learned representations directly from data. That was a very strong signal to me.

At the same time, generative models were starting to show real promise. GANs had just come out, and even though the early results were small and blurry, you could see that the network was learning something about the structure of the visual world. Faces looked like faces, bedrooms looked like bedrooms. To me, that suggested the same thing that had happened in recognition could happen in synthesis: if you have enough data and enough compute, the model can learn to generate things that traditional graphics pipelines need enormous manual effort to produce.

Video in particular felt like a natural destination. Traditional graphics is very powerful, but creating realistic content requires artists to model geometry, materials, lighting, animation, all by hand. That doesn't scale easily. Meanwhile, the world produces a huge amount of video data. If a neural network can learn from that data how things look and how they move, then you essentially have a data-driven renderer and a simulator at once.

And of course, being at NVIDIA mattered. I could see the trajectory of GPU compute. Deep learning's progress was very tightly coupled to scaling compute, and I believed that compute would keep growing. Video is one of the most compute-hungry modalities, so it made sense that as hardware improved, video generation would become feasible and eventually practical.

So it was a combination of things: the evidence from recognition, the early signs from generative models, the abundance of video data, and confidence in compute scaling. Put together, I felt deep learning was very likely to become the main way we generate visual content, including video. It took longer in some ways and happened faster in others than I expected, but the overall direction felt quite clear to me even then.

r001.rationale: The response discusses video generation broadly but does not identify generating a movie from a novel as a capability Liu envisioned.

r002.rationale: It contrasts traditional graphics’ hand-built geometry, materials, lighting, and animation with models that could generate content using less manual effort.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say that when I joined NVIDIA in 2016, the honest answer is that I didn't know. Nobody really knew. But I had a kind of conviction, and that conviction came from a few things I had seen with my own eyes.

Before NVIDIA, I spent years at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs working on computer vision the old way. You hand-design features, you build probabilistic models, you tune them. And every time the problem got slightly harder, the system broke. Then around 2012, with AlexNet, you watched a neural network trained on data just crush all of that hand-engineering. For me that was not a result about image classification. It was a lesson about where capability comes from. Capability comes from data and compute, not from the cleverness of the engineer writing the rules.

So when I asked myself, what is the hardest thing in visual computing to write rules for? The answer was generating the visual world. Graphics had spent decades doing exactly that, writing rules for light, for materials, for motion. It was beautiful work, but it required an enormous amount of human effort for every scene, every character, every physical effect. And the real world is far too rich to encode by hand. Video is the extreme case. It is not just appearance, it is dynamics, it is how things move and interact over time. If you believe the lesson of 2012, then the only way to capture that richness is to learn it from data. There is an almost unlimited supply of video of the real world. That is the data. And NVIDIA was building the compute.

Then there was GANs. When I started playing with generative adversarial networks, the images were tiny and blurry, but I remember seeing a model produce a face that did not exist and thinking, this thing has learned something about the structure of the world that nobody wrote down. If a network can learn what a face looks like, the question of whether it can learn how a face moves, how a street scene evolves, is just a question of scale. It is a harder problem, but it is not a different kind of problem.

So I would not say I predicted the timeline. In 2016, if you had asked me whether we would have the video models we have today, I would have been far too conservative. But the direction, I was fairly sure about. I thought the question was not if but when, and the when depended on how fast compute would grow and how patient we were willing to be. And frankly, joining NVIDIA was also a bet on the compute part. If you believe learning is the path, you want to be where the GPUs are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning to generate video and visual scenes, but never identifies generating a movie from a novel.

r002.rationale: It contrasts graphics that required extensive human effort to specify scenes and effects with learning visual richness from data, communicating reduced reliance on hand-authored control.

astra-6.text:
When I joined NVIDIA, my belief was that if we wanted to generate the visual world in all its complexity, we needed a system that could learn from data. Think about everything in a short video: appearance, lighting, motion, and how objects interact over time. It’s very difficult to write rules that capture all of that.

Deep learning offered a way to learn those patterns from examples. And video generation brings together two things that make that approach particularly compelling: a lot of visual data and a very large computational problem. NVIDIA was a natural place to explore that combination.

Of course, that didn’t mean convincing video generation was already solved. The question was whether models could keep improving as we gave them more data, more compute, and better architectures. I believed they could, and that made deep learning a very promising direction.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning visual patterns from data for video generation, but does not identify generating a movie from a novel as a capability.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts learned patterns with writing rules, but does not say deep learning could reduce human labor compared with traditional computer graphics.

sol-6.1.text:
When I joined NVIDIA, I believed that if we wanted computers to generate video, they needed to learn from the visual world. Video is incredibly complex—there’s motion, lighting, geometry, and all the ways objects interact. It’s very difficult to capture that richness with hand-designed rules. Deep learning offered a way to learn those patterns directly from data.

And at NVIDIA, we had the computing platform to explore that idea. My belief was that as models improved and we could train them on more data with more computation, the quality of what they generated would improve. There were still many open problems, especially keeping things consistent over time, but I felt learning from data was the most promising direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses generating video from learned visual patterns, but does not identify generating a movie from a novel.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts learning from data with hand-designed rules, but does not state that deep learning reduces human labor controlling video generation compared with traditional computer graphics.
